claims.text: Applied mechanical stress induces localized amorphization at or near grain boundaries in high-entropy alloys.
Stress-induced amorphization forms an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer retards dislocation motion.
Formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer enhances hardness and strength.
Single-phase CoCrFeMnNi exhibits inverse Hall–Petch behavior under ultra-high-vacuum conditions.
CoCrFeMnNi can serve as the single-phase alloy system for the proposed grain-size comparison.
Samples should be deformed under identical inert conditions while initial grain size is varied systematically.
Ultra-high vacuum or an inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation and mixed-metal-oxide-film formation.
Grain-boundary regions dynamically transform into an amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline phase during deformation.
Localized high strain and possible thermal effects at grain boundaries trigger a crystalline-to-amorphous transition.
The transformed near-surface layer increases resistance to shear and wear by impeding dislocation movement.
The proposed transformation is more pronounced in suitably fine-grained samples and produces inverse Hall–Petch behavior.
Fine-grained samples will form a near-surface amorphous layer under the specified deformation conditions.
Fine-grained samples will have greater hardness than coarse-grained samples.
Fine-grained samples will have lower friction than coarse-grained samples.
Coarse-grained samples will show little or no stress-induced amorphization.
Coarse-grained samples will obey classical Hall–Petch behavior and have lower hardness and wear resistance.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase high-entropy alloys tested under conditions that minimize oxidation.
In multiphase alloys or oxidizing environments, phase strengthening or oxide-layer formation may dominate the mechanical response.
The critical grain size and compositional dependence for the onset of amorphization are not established and may vary among HEA systems.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes inverse Hall–Petch behavior, but the prediction that finer grains are harder than coarse grains and the baseline statement that coarse grains are softer describe the ordinary Hall–Petch direction. Inverse Hall–Petch behavior normally denotes softening as grain size decreases below a critical scale.

The structural state is described inconsistently as amorphous, ultra-nanocrystalline, or either one. These are distinct states, so accepting either as the mediator does not cleanly test the specific claim that amorphization creates an ultra-nanocrystalline layer.
